title: Does Weight Sparsity Improve Circuit Recoverability? Replicating OpenAI's Weight-Sparse Transformer Study on GPT-2

original_idea.quick_reasoning: Clearly addresses an AI Safety problem with a reasonably scoped approach.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Plausible chain: if post-hoc pruning improves circuit recoverability, it is a cheap intervention to make deployed models more interpretable. However, the link between 'more recoverable circuits' and a specific safety outcome (what failure mode does this prevent?) is underspecified.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Requires magnitude pruning at 5 sparsity levels, running circuit discovery (attribution patching) on the IOI task for each, and measuring faithfulness metrics. This demands familiarity with both pruning pipelines and interpretability tooling (ACDC/attribution patching in TransformerLens). Advanced for beginner CS students.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Well-bounded: 5 sparsity levels, 1 task (IOI), clear metrics (edge faithfulness, circuit size). The experimental design is a clean sweep. Single GPU suffices. Could be done in 30 hours if the tooling is familiar.

novelty.reasoning: OpenAI published 'Weight-sparse transformers have interpretable circuits' (arXiv:2511.13653, Nov 2025), which directly trains weight-sparse GPT-2-style transformers and measures circuit recoverability across sparsity levels. The proposed study is essentially a replication of this existing work on the same model architecture (GPT-2) with the same methodology (attribution patching on IOI at multiple sparsity levels). The core question—does weight sparsity improve circuit recoverability—is answered by the existing paper, which finds circuits ~16x smaller at matched loss. A replication adds marginal value but the research question is largely addressed.
